unit.title: Perform advanced welding using gas metal arc welding process GMAW -(Metal inert gas MIG)

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Shanice is leading a MIG job on a steel frame that must be welded to a WPS (welding procedure specification). What should she do before any welding starts?
options: Let each welder choose the settings they are used to
Check the WPS and brief the team on its ranges
Start welding and write the WPS when the job is done
Use the machine's last settings to save some time

questions.stem: What is the difference between a WPS and a PQR (procedure qualification record)?
options: The WPS is for steel and the PQR is for aluminium
The PQR is the client's order and the WPS is the bill
They are two names for the same welding document
The PQR records the test weld that proves the WPS

questions.stem: A 12 mm steel butt joint is to be filled in the flat position, and a high rate of deposit is wanted. Which MIG transfer mode is best for this job?
options: Spray transfer with an argon-rich gas
Short-circuit transfer with 100% CO2
Short-circuit transfer at the lowest voltage
Globular transfer with a long stick-out

questions.stem: Why is short-circuit (dip) transfer on thick plate a risk for lack of fusion?
options: It puts so much heat into the plate that it burns through
It needs pure argon, which cannot shield thick plate
Its low heat may not melt the sides of the joint fully
It makes heavy slag that gets trapped between the passes

questions.stem: Why is ordinary spray transfer not used for a vertical-up butt weld on steel?
options: The wire cannot be fed fast enough in that position
Spray transfer only works on aluminium, never on steel
The large, fluid weld pool would run out of the joint
The arc goes out whenever the gun points upwards

questions.stem: Which MIG mode gives spray-type fusion on thicker plate and can still be used in all positions?
options: Pulsed spray
Globular transfer
Short arc at a very low wire speed
Spray transfer with 100% CO2

questions.stem: A welder tries to get spray transfer on steel using 100% carbon dioxide (CO2). What will happen?
options: Smooth spray transfer with less spatter than argon mixes
Spray transfer, but only when welding in the vertical position
No arc at all, because carbon dioxide does not carry current
Globular transfer with heavy spatter, not a true spray

questions.stem: Which shielding gas is generally used for MIG welding stainless steel?
options: 100% carbon dioxide, the same as for mild steel
Argon with a small amount of oxygen or CO2
Pure oxygen, to burn off the chromium oxide
Acetylene mixed with argon to give extra heat

questions.stem: Why might an argon-helium mix be chosen for MIG welding thick aluminium?
options: It is cheaper than pure argon and easier to store
It lets the welder use steel wire on aluminium
It removes the need to clean the oxide off the plate
It gives a hotter arc and deeper, wider fusion

questions.stem: A job needs about 50 minutes of arc time, with the gas flowing at 15 L/min. About how much gas is used while welding?
options: 65 litres
750 litres
3.3 litres
7 500 litres

questions.stem: In the wire classification ER70S-6, what does the "6" mainly tell you?
options: The wire diameter is 0.6 mm
It may be used in six positions
Its make-up, including deoxidisers
Feed it at 6 metres per minute

questions.stem: Why is ER70S-6 wire often chosen over ER70S-3 for steel with light mill scale or rust?
options: It has more deoxidisers to deal with the dirt
It is thinner, so it melts through rust faster
It needs no shielding gas, so dirt does not matter
It has no copper coat, so it cannot react with rust

questions.stem: Which wire feed set-up is best for feeding soft 1.2 mm aluminium wire through a standard (push) torch?
options: U-groove rolls and a plastic (PTFE or nylon) liner
Knurled rolls and a steel liner at high roll pressure
V-groove rolls and a steel liner, the same as for steel
Any rolls, with the spool brake set as tight as it goes

questions.stem: Why is the contact tip for aluminium wire often one size bigger than the wire?
options: So that the wire can be fed backwards after a weld
So that less welding current passes into the wire
Hot aluminium wire expands and can seize in a tight tip
So that the shielding gas can pass through the tip

questions.stem: Which gun technique is normally used for MIG welding aluminium?
options: Pull (drag), to bury the oxide in the weld
Push, for good gas cover and cleaning ahead
Pull, with the gun at 45° to the line of weld
Weave with long pauses at each side of the joint

questions.stem: When MIG welding stainless steel, why is heat input kept low and the interpass temperature controlled?
options: To stop the stainless steel from turning magnetic
To make the bead darker so that it matches the plate
So that the shielding gas flow can be turned down
To limit distortion and keep its corrosion resistance

questions.stem: On a MIG set using short-circuit transfer, what does adding more inductance generally do?
options: Gives a colder arc with more spatter and a narrow bead
Gives a wetter, flatter bead with less spatter
Raises the wire feed speed by the same amount
Changes the polarity from DCEP to DCEN

questions.stem: Heat input (kJ/mm) = (volts × amps × 60) ÷ (travel speed in mm/min × 1000). A run is made at 24 V, 200 A and 400 mm/min. What is the heat input?
options: 0.72 kJ/mm
7.2 kJ/mm
1.2 kJ/mm
0.12 kJ/mm

questions.stem: A WPS gives a heat input range of 0.8 to 1.5 kJ/mm. Your test run works out at 2.1 kJ/mm. What should you do?
options: Carry on, because more heat always makes a stronger weld
Turn the voltage up to bring the figure down
Slow the travel speed to bring the heat input down
Change settings or travel faster to bring it into range

questions.stem: What happens to the welding current if the contact-tip-to-work distance (stick-out) is made longer while the wire speed stays the same?
options: The current rises and penetration gets deeper
The voltage drops to zero and the arc goes out
The current falls and penetration gets less
Nothing changes, because the machine holds it

questions.stem: For a 10 mm steel butt joint in the vertical position (3G), which way of welding gives the best fusion with short-circuit MIG?
options: Vertical down, as fast as possible
Vertical down with a long stick-out
Vertical up, with a slight weave
Horizontal runs across the joint

questions.stem: When is vertical-down MIG welding a sensible choice?
options: On thick structural plate that needs full penetration
On any joint, because it is quicker and always stronger
On overhead joints in thick plate, to stop sagging
On thin sheet, where burn-through is the main risk

questions.stem: When MIG welding a fillet overhead (4F), which change helps stop the weld pool from sagging?
options: A smaller pool: lower settings, faster travel
Higher voltage and a slower travel speed
A longer stick-out and a wide, slow weave
Changing to spray transfer for more heat

questions.stem: A 12 mm single-V butt with a backing strip is to be MIG welded in the 3G position. Why does the WPS give a root gap?
options: So the backing strip can be knocked off after welding
So the root run can fuse both plates and the backing
So the plates are free to move while they are welded
So that less filler wire is needed to fill the joint

questions.stem: Which method best reduces distortion on a long MIG weld on a thin steel panel?
options: One continuous run from one end, as fast as you can
Welding from both ends to meet in the middle
Welding one side fully before tacking the other
Backstep or skip welding in short, spaced runs

questions.stem: Why are parts sometimes set at a small angle (pre-set) before a single-sided weld?
options: So that the weld can be made with less filler wire
To make room for the gun nozzle down at the root
So that weld shrinkage pulls them back into line
To let the shielding gas escape from the joint

questions.stem: A MIG fillet weld looks smooth, but a break test shows the weld metal has not fused to the plate. What is this defect called?
options: Undercut at the toe
Lack of fusion (cold lap)
A crater crack
Excess reinforcement

questions.stem: MIG welds made near an open roller door show porosity, but welds inside the booth are sound. What is the most likely cause?
options: Wind blowing the shielding gas away
The wire feed speed set too low
The work clamp on the wrong side
The plate being thicker near the door

questions.stem: MIG welds keep showing a small crack in the crater at the end of each run. Which practice helps prevent it?
options: Fill the crater before breaking the arc
Stop the arc suddenly and pull the gun away
Turn the gas off as soon as the arc stops
Speed up the travel towards the end of the run

questions.stem: The wire keeps stubbing into the plate and pushing the gun back. Which setting is most likely wrong?
options: Voltage too high for the wire speed
Voltage too low for the wire speed
Gas flow too high for the nozzle
Polarity set to DCEP

questions.stem: As team leader, when should you inspect a multi-pass MIG weld?
options: Only at the end, once the cap is finished
Only if the client asks for a test
Before, during and after welding
Only on the first weld of each day

questions.stem: The specification limits undercut depth. You find undercut deeper than allowed on a fillet weld. What should happen?
options: Accept it, because undercut does not affect strength
Paint over it so that the client cannot see it
Grind out every weld on the job and scrap the part
Record it and repair it to an approved procedure

questions.stem: Which test shows the inside of a weld by cutting a cross-section, polishing it and etching it?
options: A visual inspection
A fillet break test
A macro-etch test
A hardness test

questions.stem: Why is a guided bend test used on a butt weld test plate?
options: To open up hidden flaws by bending the weld
To find the weld's exact tensile strength
To measure the height of the weld cap
To check that the plate was cut square

questions.stem: A drawing calls for a 6 mm fillet weld (leg length). Using throat = 0.707 × leg, what is the throat thickness of a flat-faced, equal-leg fillet?
options: About 8.5 mm
About 4.2 mm
About 6.0 mm
About 3.0 mm

questions.stem: A job requires MIG welding galvanised (zinc-coated) steel. Which control is best?
options: Weld as normal, but work fast to keep the fume low
Weld outside with no mask, as the wind clears the fume
Weld as normal, then drink milk to stop fume fever
Remove the zinc near the joint and use fume extraction

questions.stem: You are planning MIG welding inside a large steel tank. Which control must be in your plan?
options: A permit, gas testing and forced ventilation
A bigger gas cylinder so the welder does not run out
A higher gas flow so the shielding is not lost inside
A dark-shade helmet for everyone outside the tank

questions.stem: Why does MIG welding aluminium with argon often need more ozone control than MIG welding steel?
options: Aluminium gives off cyanide gas when it melts
Argon turns into carbon monoxide in the arc
Aluminium wire contains lead that turns to fume
The strong ultraviolet light makes more ozone

questions.stem: A welder reports that the wire feeds in jerks during a long run. Which check should you make first?
options: Change the shielding gas to pure CO2
Turn the voltage up two steps
Check the liner, tip, rolls and spool brake
Shorten the work lead by half

questions.stem: A MIG set is rated 250 A at 40% duty cycle (on a 10-minute cycle). What does this mean?
options: At 250 A it may weld for 4 minutes in every 10
It can weld for 40 minutes at 250 A without a rest
It uses 40% less power than a 250 A stick welder
It welds at 40% of 250 A, which is 100 A

questions.stem: A new team member is welding outside the WPS voltage range because "it looks better". As team leader, what do you do?
options: Stop the work, explain the WPS and check the welds made
Let them carry on as long as the welds look neat
Change the WPS so that it matches their settings
Leave it and report it at the end of the month

questions.stem: Which record should be kept for each weld on a job made to a specification?
options: The times of the welder's lunch breaks
The colour of the welder's overalls
Welder, WPS, wire batch and results
The price paid for each spool of wire

questions.stem: Which job is the best fit for MIG rather than TIG?
options: A thin stainless food tray that the customer will see
A thin-wall aluminium bicycle frame joint
The root of a small stainless pipe with a purge
Long fillet welds on a 10 mm steel frame

questions.stem: A multi-pass MIG weld must be stopped and restarted part way. How should the restart be made?
options: Start on top of the old crater with low settings
Grind the stop to a taper and start just before it
Start 50 mm past the stop and leave the gap open
Restart cold, then hammer the joint flat

questions.stem: Before MIG welding aluminium, what is the correct way to clean it?
options: Use a wire brush that was used on mild steel
Grind with the disc used on steel, then degrease
Degrease, then use a clean stainless steel brush
Wash with water and weld it while it is damp

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What do the letters WPS stand for?
What do the letters PQR stand for?
Name the MIG transfer mode in which the machine switches between a high peak current and a low background current many times a second.
What is the position code for a groove (butt) weld on plate in the vertical position?
What is the position code for a fillet weld made in the overhead position?
A job needs 40 minutes of arc time at a gas flow of 18 L/min. How many litres of gas is that?
Using throat = 0.7 × leg length, what is the throat thickness of an 8 mm fillet weld?
Name the MIG gun that carries a small reel of wire on the gun itself, often used to feed soft aluminium wire.
Name the test in which a fillet weld is pressed or hammered over until it breaks, so that the fusion and root can be seen.
Which gas, mixed with argon, gives a hotter arc for MIG welding thick aluminium?
What is the name of the method where short runs are welded in the opposite direction to the overall progress of the weld, to control distortion?
Using heat input (kJ/mm) = (V × A × 60) ÷ (travel speed in mm/min × 1000), work out the heat input at 20 V, 150 A and 300 mm/min.
What is the name of the strip of metal fitted behind a butt joint so that the root can be fully penetrated without falling through?
Name the test that uses a coloured liquid and a white developer to show cracks that break the surface.
Name the transfer mode in which large, irregular drops, bigger than the wire, fall across the arc.

essays.stem: Describe the four MIG metal transfer modes (short-circuit, globular, spray and pulsed spray). Then say which mode you would choose for each of these jobs, and why: a 2 mm steel sheet panel, the fill passes of a 12 mm flat butt joint, and a 10 mm structural joint welded vertical up.
essays.modelAnswer: In short-circuit transfer the wire touches the pool many times a second and each touch puts a small drop in. It is low heat and works in all positions on thin metal. In globular transfer large, irregular drops fall across the arc. It gives spatter and is mainly seen with CO2 at higher settings. In spray transfer, with an argon-rich gas and high current, fine drops fly across a steady arc. It gives deep fusion and a high deposit rate but a large, fluid pool, so it is used flat and for horizontal fillets. Pulsed spray switches between a peak and a low background current, giving spray fusion with less average heat, so it can be used in all positions. For 2 mm sheet I would use short-circuit, to avoid burn-through. For the 12 mm flat fill passes I would use spray, for speed and fusion. For the 10 mm vertical-up joint I would use pulsed spray if the set has it; otherwise short-circuit with care at the sidewalls.
markingPoints: Short-circuit: wire touches the pool, low heat, all positions, thin metal
Globular: large irregular drops, spatter, mostly CO2 at higher settings
Spray: argon-rich gas, high current, fine drops, flat and horizontal only
Pulsed spray: peak and background current, lower average heat, all positions
Sensible choices with reasons: sheet short-circuit, flat fill spray, vertical pulsed (or short-circuit with care)

essays.stem: You are the team leader for a MIG job on a structural steel frame that must be welded to a WPS. Describe how you would plan the job and brief the team before welding starts.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would read the drawing, the specification and the WPS, and list the joints, weld sizes, positions and any tests. I would check that each welder is qualified for the process, position and thickness in the WPS. I would check the materials against the drawing and the wire type and gas against the WPS, and make sure there is enough of each. I would check every MIG set: cables, gun, liner, contact tips, rolls, gas hose and regulator, and the earth clamp. I would arrange hot work controls: screens, a fire extinguisher, clear combustibles and fume extraction. I would plan the weld sequence to control distortion and mark the hold points where I will inspect, such as fit-up, after the root and after the cap. At the briefing I would explain the job, the WPS ranges, the sequence, the inspection points and who does what, and check they understand. I would set up the weld record sheet before we start.
markingPoints: Reads the drawing, specification and WPS; lists joints, sizes, positions and tests
Checks welders' qualifications against the WPS
Checks materials, wire, gas and equipment before starting
Plans hot work and fume controls and the weld sequence for distortion
Briefs the team on WPS ranges, hold points and roles; prepares records

essays.stem: Explain how a MIG set must be changed to weld aluminium instead of mild steel, and give the reason for each change.
essays.modelAnswer: Aluminium wire is soft, so it can bend and tangle (birdnest) in a long steel liner. I would use a spool gun or a push-pull torch, or keep the torch short and straight. I would fit U-groove drive rolls and a plastic (PTFE or nylon) liner so the wire is not crushed or shaved, and set the roll pressure light. I would fit a contact tip made for aluminium, often one size larger, because the hot wire expands and can seize. I would change the gas to pure argon, or argon with helium for thick plate, because active gases such as CO2 must not be used on aluminium. The wire must be an aluminium grade that suits the parent alloy, as the WPS says. The metal must be degreased and then brushed with a clean stainless brush used only for aluminium, to remove the oxide. I would use a push angle and a faster travel speed, because aluminium conducts heat away quickly, and fill the crater at the end to avoid cracks.
markingPoints: Spool gun or push-pull torch (or short straight torch) because the wire is soft
U-groove rolls, plastic liner, light roll pressure
Aluminium contact tip, often oversized, because the wire expands
Pure argon or argon-helium, never CO2 mixes; matching filler wire
Degrease and stainless-brush the oxide; push technique; fill the crater

essays.stem: Describe how you would MIG weld a 10 mm single-V butt joint with a backing strip in the vertical position (3G), welding upwards, from fit-up to the cap.
essays.modelAnswer: I would check the bevel angle, root face and root gap against the WPS, clean the joint to bright metal and tack the backing strip tight to both plates so that there is no gap under the root. I would set the machine to the WPS for vertical welding, test on scrap and check the gas flow. I would weld upwards, holding the gun at about 90° to the plate across the joint and pointing slightly up (about 5–15°). For the root, I would make sure the arc melts into both plate edges and the backing, with a small side-to-side movement. I would clean every pass with a wire brush or grinder before the next one, removing any silica islands and high spots. For the fill passes I would use a slight weave, pausing at each side to fuse the sidewalls and avoid cold lap. The cap would be a weave just past the edges of the bevel, with a small, even reinforcement and no undercut. I would check the interpass temperature and inspect each pass.
markingPoints: Checks fit-up to the WPS; backing strip tight; joint clean
Sets and tests the machine for vertical-up; checks gas
Correct gun angles; root fused into both edges and the backing
Cleans between passes; weave with pauses at the sidewalls to avoid cold lap
Cap just past the bevel edges, even reinforcement, no undercut; inspects each pass

essays.stem: Explain what heat input is, how voltage, current and travel speed change it, and why a WPS may set limits on it. Include a worked example.
essays.modelAnswer: Heat input is the amount of arc energy put into each millimetre of weld. It is worked out as volts × amps × 60, divided by the travel speed in mm/min × 1000, which gives kJ/mm. Raising the voltage or the current raises the heat input. Travelling faster lowers it, because the same energy is spread over a longer length. For example, at 22 V, 180 A and 300 mm/min: 22 × 180 × 60 = 237 600, and 300 × 1000 = 300 000, so the heat input is about 0.79 kJ/mm. A WPS sets limits because too little heat input can cause lack of fusion and a hard, brittle zone next to the weld, which can crack. Too much heat input can cause distortion, a coarse grain and lower toughness, and on stainless steel a loss of corrosion resistance. The welder must keep the settings and travel speed within the WPS and record them.
markingPoints: Defines heat input as arc energy per length of weld (kJ/mm) with the formula
Volts and amps raise it; faster travel lowers it
Correct worked example
Too low: lack of fusion, hard zone, cracking risk
Too high: distortion, lower toughness, stainless corrosion loss; stay within WPS and record

essays.stem: Explain why MIG welding causes distortion, and describe the methods you would use to control it on a fabricated steel frame.
essays.modelAnswer: Distortion happens because the weld and the metal next to it expand when hot and then shrink as they cool. The shrinking weld pulls the parts out of line, causing angular distortion, bowing or twisting. To control it, I would not over-weld: I would make welds the size on the drawing and no larger, because extra weld metal means more shrinkage. I would tack the frame square, with tacks evenly spaced, and check the diagonals before welding. I would clamp it to a flat table or use a jig. I would balance the welding: weld opposite sides in turn and work from the centre outwards. On long welds I would use backstep or skip welding. Where shrinkage is known, I would pre-set the parts at a small angle so that they pull back into line. I would check squareness during the job and correct early, and record what worked for the next frame.
markingPoints: Explains expansion and shrinkage as the cause
Weld only to the size needed
Tack evenly, clamp or use a jig, check diagonals
Balanced sequence, backstep or skip welding
Pre-setting; checks squareness during the job

essays.stem: Several MIG fillet test pieces from your team have failed break tests because of lack of fusion. Explain how you would find the cause, put it right and record what was done.
essays.modelAnswer: I would stop the production welding on that joint type and keep the failed pieces. I would look at the broken faces to see where the fusion was missing: at the root, on one leg or between passes. I would check the machine settings used against the WPS, especially voltage and wire speed, because settings that are too low give a cold weld. I would check the transfer mode, because short-circuit on thick plate is a common cause. I would watch each welder's technique: gun angle, stick-out, travel speed, and whether the wire was leading the pool or riding on top of it. I would check the joint fit-up and cleanliness, and the contact tip and earth connection. Once I found the cause, I would correct the settings or technique, coach the welders and have them weld new test pieces until they pass. I would record the failure, the cause found, the action taken and the retest results, and report it to my supervisor.
markingPoints: Stops the work and keeps the evidence; studies the fracture faces
Checks settings and transfer mode against the WPS
Watches technique: angles, stick-out, travel speed, wire on the leading edge
Corrects, coaches and retests until pieces pass
Records failure, cause, action and retest; reports to the supervisor

essays.stem: Compare visual inspection, the fillet break test, the macro-etch test and the guided bend test. For each, say what it shows and when you would use it.
essays.modelAnswer: Visual inspection is done on every weld, before, during and after welding. It shows surface faults such as undercut, porosity, overlap, cracks, the wrong size or poor shape, and uses gauges to check sizes. It cannot see inside the weld. The fillet break test is a destructive test where a fillet weld is broken over so the fracture face can be seen. It shows lack of root fusion, porosity and slag inside. It is used for welder training and qualification. The macro-etch test cuts a cross-section, which is polished and etched so that the fusion lines, penetration and passes can be seen. It is used to check a procedure or the penetration and leg sizes of fillets. The guided bend test bends a strip cut from a butt weld around a former. Any lack of fusion or other flaw opens up. It is used to qualify welders and procedures on butt welds. The last three destroy the sample, so they are done on test pieces, not on the client's job.
markingPoints: Visual: every weld, surface faults and size, cannot see inside
Fillet break: fracture face shows root fusion, porosity and slag
Macro-etch: cross-section shows penetration, fusion lines and passes
Guided bend: opens up flaws in butt welds; used for qualification
Notes that the last three are destructive and done on test pieces

essays.stem: Describe the main hazards when MIG welding galvanised steel, stainless steel and aluminium at the Centre, and the controls you would put in your risk assessment.
essays.modelAnswer: Galvanised steel gives off zinc oxide fume, which can cause metal fume fever, a flu-like illness. I would remove the coating near the joint where the job allows, and use local fume extraction. Stainless steel fume contains chromium and nickel compounds, which can harm the lungs and can cause cancer, so extraction close to the arc is needed, with a suitable respirator where extraction is not enough. MIG welding aluminium with argon gives very strong ultraviolet light, which makes ozone and burns skin and eyes quickly, so full cover clothing, the correct filter shade and good ventilation are needed. For all three: screens to protect others from arc flash, fire precautions with an extinguisher at hand, cylinders chained upright and checked for leaks, gloves and clothing kept dry, and cables checked. In a closed space, shielding gas can push out oxygen, so a permit, gas testing and ventilation are needed. I would follow the maker's instructions, the SDS and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Galvanised: zinc fume and metal fume fever; remove coating and extract
Stainless: chromium and nickel fume; local extraction, respirator if needed
Aluminium: strong UV and ozone; cover skin, correct shade, ventilation
General: screens, fire precautions, cylinder safety, dry PPE, cable checks
Confined spaces: oxygen displacement; permit, gas testing, ventilation; SDS and Centre rules

essays.stem: Explain what you would put in a written report to your supervisor at the end of a MIG fabrication job, and why each part matters.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start with the job details: the job number, the client, the drawing and the WPS used, so that the report can be traced. I would list who welded which joints, because each weld must be traceable to a qualified welder. I would record the wire type and batch, the gas and the settings used, to show the WPS was followed. I would give the inspection and test results, including any defects found, how they were repaired and the retest results, because this proves the quality. I would note the time taken against the plan and the materials used, so that future jobs can be estimated better. I would record any safety incidents or near misses and any equipment faults, so that they can be followed up. I would finish with problems met and suggestions for next time. The report should be clear, dated and signed, with photos or sketches where they help.
markingPoints: Job details, drawing and WPS for traceability
Welders, consumables and settings used
Inspection and test results, repairs and retests
Time and materials against the plan; incidents and equipment faults
Lessons and suggestions; clear, dated and signed

practical1.title: Plan, weld and test MIG fillet joints in the vertical (3F) and overhead (4F) positions to a WPS
practical1.brief: As a team, read the WPS the assessor gives you for short-circuit or pulsed MIG on 10 mm carbon steel and write a short plan: the settings range, the gun angles, the weld sequence, the inspection points and who does what. Set up and check two MIG stations. Each member welds one tee joint in the vertical position, welding upwards (3F), and one tee joint overhead (4F), each about 150 mm long, to the WPS, while the assessor watches. Members take turns to act as team leader at each station: checking the settings against the WPS, inspecting each weld with a fillet gauge and recording the results. Then break-test the vertical joints in the press or vice, as the assessor directs, and record what each fracture face shows. Complete a weld record sheet for every joint. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the welds, the record sheets and the clean-up are finished.
materials: Carbon steel plate, 10 mm, cut into tee joint pieces about 150 mm × 75 mm (2 joints per member)
WPS from the assessor, plan sheet and weld record sheets
Two MIG sets with ER70S-6 wire (1.0 mm or as the WPS states) and argon/CO2 mix gas
Fillet weld gauges, steel rule, wire brushes and an angle grinder
Positioning stand or clamp to hold joints vertical and overhead
Press or heavy vice and hammer for the break test, as the assessor provides
photos: The team plan and the WPS, with the settings range marked
Both MIG stations set up and checked, with screens and extinguisher
A member welding a vertical-up joint in full PPE
A member welding an overhead joint in full PPE
All finished joints laid out and labelled with each member's name
A fillet gauge on a finished weld
The broken vertical joints showing the fracture faces
checklist: Read the WPS correctly and helped write the plan
Checked the MIG set (gun, liner, tip, rolls, gas, earth) before welding
Set and kept the settings within the WPS range
Made a vertical-up fillet with even legs, good fusion and no excessive undercut
Made an overhead fillet without sagging, overlap or excessive spatter
Inspected welds with a fillet gauge and recorded results accurately
Led the station in turn: checked others' settings and gave clear instructions

practical2.title: Fabricate a square steel frame with MIG, controlling distortion, and inspect it to the drawing
practical2.brief: As a team, make a rectangular frame about 800 mm × 500 mm from 40 mm × 40 mm square hollow section (SHS), with a 10 mm base plate welded to each corner, to the drawing the assessor gives you. First, write a plan: the cutting list, the joint preparation, the tack and weld sequence you will use to control distortion, the MIG settings from the WPS and who does what. Cut and prepare the parts, set them on a flat table or jig and tack them, then check the diagonals and flatness before full welding. Weld to your sequence, using short-circuit transfer for the positional welds and, if the Centre's set allows, spray transfer for the flat fillets on the base plates. Each member cuts or prepares at least one part and welds at least one corner. Measure the finished frame (sizes, diagonals, twist and weld sizes) and write a short inspection report comparing it with the drawing. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the frame, the report and the clean-up are finished.
materials: 40 mm × 40 mm SHS, about 3 m (wall thickness as the assessor gives)
Four pieces of 10 mm carbon steel plate, about 100 mm × 100 mm
Drawing and WPS from the assessor, plan sheet and inspection report sheet
MIG set with steel wire and suitable gas
Cut-off saw or bandsaw, angle grinder, files
Flat welding table or jig, clamps, squares, tape measure, fillet gauge
photos: The written plan with the cutting list and the weld sequence
The parts cut, prepared and labelled
The frame tacked on the table, with a tape measuring the diagonals
A member welding a corner in full PPE
The finished frame on the table, showing flatness
Measuring the finished diagonals and weld sizes
checklist: Helped plan a weld sequence that controls distortion
Cut and prepared parts to the cutting list within tolerance
Tacked square and checked diagonals before full welding
Followed the planned sequence and the WPS settings
Made sound corner welds with good fusion and correct size
Measured the finished frame accurately and recorded it
Took a fair share of the work and communicated clearly with the team
Wore the right PPE throughout and left the area safe and tidy
safety: Wear safety glasses and a face shield when cutting and grinding; check guards and discs
Weld behind screens with an extinguisher at hand and combustibles cleared
Treat all cut and welded parts as hot; use gloves or tongs and mark hot work
Lift long lengths and the finished frame with two people
Use fume extraction close to the arc
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
